Those people who perform— meaning they practice— a "terrible" austerity (tapas), such as climbing heated stones and the like, which is not ordained by the *śāstra*— that is, not prescribed by the Veda through direct perception or inference— but is instead taught by what is non-*śāstra*, namely the scriptures of Buddha and others;
and who do so while being fully possessed by hypocrisy (*dambha*)— the display of one's own piety— and egoism (*ahaṃkāra*)— the wicked conceit that "I alone am superior."

The perfection of yoga is the capacity to produce detachment without effort. "Desire" (*kāma*) refers to longing for an object that is being craved; "passion" (*rāga*) is the attachment characterized by a constant state of fixation upon that [object]. It is endowed with the power [to endure] that cause—namely, the strength consisting in the capacity to withstand extreme suffering.
"Desire" is the yearning for an object;
"passion" is the intense clinging in the form of perpetual adherence to it.

"Power" is the insistence that "I shall certainly accomplish this," or it means being endowed with those [qualities]. For this very reason, they do not turn back even when confronted with suffering caused by force.

By means of futile fasts and other such practices, they emaciate— the group of elements residing within the body, which has evolved into the form of the aggregate of the physical body and the senses; being mindless and devoid of discrimination, they likewise emaciate Me, who am situated within the body as the Experiencer, by emaciating the body which is the object of experience.
Or rather, they are those who, by transgressing My command, emaciate Me—the Lord who dwells within the body as the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) and the witness of the intellect and its modifications.

Turned away from all worldly enjoyments in this life, destined for the lowest state hereafter, and fallen from all human goals, they possess a demonic resolve; that is, they possess a resolve in the form of perversion which contradicts the meaning of the Vedas, yet they appear in the form of human beings.

Know—that is, recognize—as *asuras* even those who appear otherwise, because they perform the deeds of *asuras*, so that you may avoid them. Since the certainty [of their nature] is demonic, all the functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) preceded by that [certainty] are also demonic.
Furthermore, it should be understood that although humans devoid of the *asura* species are not explicitly called *asuras*, they are to be known as *asuras* solely by virtue of their actions. (5–6)
Viśvanātha:
Regarding that which you asked— namely, "What is the final goal of those who, casting aside the scriptural injunctions, worship with faith while devoid of desire for enjoyment"—
he says, "Not according to scripture," in two verses, to state the answer to that.

"They perform" (tapyante) means they practice "terrible asceticism" (ghoraṃ tapaḥ), which causes fear to living beings; this is an elliptical expression that includes the performance of recitations, sacrifices, and so forth that are contrary to the scriptures.
The absence of acting out of desire and the state of being endowed with faith are understood by themselves [from the context].
They are "joined with hypocrisy and egoism."
For it is impossible to transgress the injunctions of the scriptures without hypocrisy and egoism.

"Desire" (kāma) is one's longing for things such as sovereignty over one's own immortality; "passion" (rāga) is attachment to asceticism; "power" (bala) is the capacity to perform austerities, like that of Hiraṇyakaśipu and others.
Possessed of these, they [the demons] regard that which resides in the body—the Self—by way of identifying with the body.

Weakening—that is, making emaciated—the multitude, the collection, of the elements such as earth and so forth, and causing suffering to me and to the individual soul (jīva) who is a portion of myself; they possess convictions born of envy, meaning they are established in the very final state of the Asuras. //5-6//
Baladeva, confirming what was stated in the previous chapter— that there is never an escape from the miserable state for those outside the Vedic fold— says in two verses beginning with "aśāstreṇa":
"Those who perform, that is, practice, terrible austerity— which causes pain to others— prescribed by their own scriptures that are contrary to the Vedas (*aśāstra*),
[driven] by desire and passion (longing for sense objects) and by the stubborn persistence that 'this can be accomplished by me' through the power of perfected beings."

Those mindless ones— devoid of the scriptural discernment of wisdom— who, by means of futile fasting and other such practices, emaciate the collection of elements (the aggregate of earth and so forth) that constitute the body and reside within it as its initiators, and who likewise emaciate Me, the Inner Controller situated within the body, out of contempt; they are outside the Veda and possess demonic resolve.
The meaning is that by the certainty [of their nature], one should know them to be asuras; thus, for those previously mentioned, a miserable rebirth is indeed unavoidable.

However, for those who worship yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, and so forth with faith born of their own nature, if there occurs the powerful grace of a true Vedic follower, the destruction of the asura-nature will surely happen through scriptural faith.
But since the sacrifice to the gods is essentially characterized by *sattva*, it is established that when their favor is obtained, the scriptural path becomes easily accessible. //5-6//
Furthermore, the food dear to everyone is also of three kinds; likewise for sacrifice, austerity, and charity—listen now to this distinction between them. (17.7)

Śrīdhara: In order to demonstrate the distinction between the *sāttvika* and other types [of dispositions] even through differences such as food and so forth, he says in thirteen verses beginning with "But food...
The food, such as grain and the like, which is dear to every person, is of three kinds according to their respective natures;
likewise, sacrifice, austerity, and charity are also of three kinds—listen to this division of them which is about to be described.

And this is stated for the purpose of explaining that one must exert effort toward the increase of *sattva* by abandoning food, sacrifice, and other practices characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*, and by cultivating those characterized by *sattva*. //7//
Madhusūdana:

Since it is established that those who are characterized by *sattva* are the gods (*devas*), while those characterized by *rajas* and *tamas* are the *asuras* due to their perverted nature, [the Lord] speaks of the threefold nature of food, sacrifice, austerity, and charity— beginning with the word "food"— for the purpose of acquiring the *sāttvika* qualities and abandoning the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* ones.
Not only is faith alone threefold;
food as well, which is dear to everyone, is likewise threefold, because everything consists of the three *guṇas* and a fourth category is impossible.
Just as food for visible purposes is threefold, so too sacrifice, austerity, and charity, which have invisible purposes, are also threefold.

In this context, we shall explain sacrifice (*yajña*). According to the authors of the ritual manuals (*kalpakāras*), sacrifice is defined as the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity; thus, the etymological definition (*nirukta*) is that sacrifice is the relinquishment of a substance with reference to a deity. Furthermore, because it is enjoined by the verbal roots *yajati* and *juhoti*, it is of two kinds: the *yāga* (offering) and the *homa* (oblation). The *yājas* are those performed while standing, ending with the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, and accompanied by both the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses. The *homas* are performed while seated, ending with the utterance of *svāhā*, and are devoid of both the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses.
"Juhoti" is explained by the authors of the ritual manuals (*kalpakāras*) as being denoted by the term "sacrifice" (*yajña*).

"Austerity" (*tapas*) is the emaciation of the body and the senses through practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances. "Giving" (*dāna*) is the relinquishment of one's own ownership with the result of transferring it to the ownership of another.
Listen to this explanation by me concerning the sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic distinctions among those [categories of] food, sacrifice, austerity, and charity. //7//
Viśvanātha:

Thus, the meaning of this section is that all those who abandon the injunctions of the scriptures and act according to their own whims— as described in the previous chapter— and those in this chapter who worship Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, and so forth according to the demonic scriptural injunctions, as well as those who perform asceticism and other such acts contrary to the scriptures, all of them indeed fall within the demonic creation (āsura-sarga).

Nevertheless, because the food and other items to be described hereafter are of three kinds, one should personally discern and understand the divine and demoniacal creations of those who possess them accordingly; thus [the Lord] says in the thirteen verses beginning with "But food," starting with "Food indeed.
Baladeva: This being the case, He describes the threefold nature of that food and so forth with the words "But food indeed.
For everyone, whatever food—such as grain—is dear to them according to their faith (*śraddhā*), that food is likewise of three kinds.
In this way, sacrifices and so forth are also threefold;
[this applies] to those four, beginning with food. //7//

Food that increases life-span, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy; which is savory, unctuous, substantial, and agreeable to the heart—such food is dear to those characterized by sattva. 17.8
Śrīdhara: Regarding that, he explains the threefold nature of food with the three verses beginning with "āyuḥ.
*Āyuḥ* is life;
*sattva* is vigor.
Strength is power;
health is freedom from disease;
and happiness is clarity of mind.
Delight is a state of relish;
they cause the increase of life-span and so forth, specifically bringing about growth; and they are savory, meaning they possess flavor.
"Smooth" means endowed with oiliness;
"stable" means remaining for a long time in the body by virtue of their essential strength;
"pleasing to the heart" means they are heart-captivating from the mere sight of them.
Foods of this kind—such as those that are chewed and eaten—are dear to those of sattvic nature. //8//
Madhusūdana:
The classification of food, sacrifice, austerity, and charity is explained by fifteen [verses].
Among those, the classification of food is explained by three [verses], beginning with "Life" (āyuḥ).

Longevity (*āyus*) is long life; vitality (*sattva*) is mental fortitude, which brings about a state of being unchanging even amidst intense suffering; strength (*bala*) is physical capacity, which serves as the cause for the absence of fatigue in one's appropriate tasks;
and health (*ārogya*) is the absence of disease.

Satisfaction (*sukha*) is the joy immediately following a meal; contentment (*tṛpti*) is the absence of lack of appetite at the time of eating and the intensification of desire for them. These are the causes of their specific increase.

They are savory (*rasya*), meaning they are to be tasted and are characterized primarily by sweet flavor (*madhura-rasa*); they are unctuous (*snigdha*), being endowed with natural or acquired oiliness;
and they are stable (*sthira*), remaining in the body for a long duration due to their constituent parts such as taste and so forth.
Delightful and heart-pleasing, free from visible and invisible defects such as foul odors and impurity—
foods consisting of what is chewed, sucked, licked, and drunk are dear to those of sattvic nature.
By these signs, one should know the sattvic person and their state of being sattvic.
The meaning is that these should be accepted by those who desire them. //8//
Viśvanātha:
It is well known that the lifespan of those who consume *sāttvika* food increases.
*Sattva* is enthusiasm (*utsāha*).
Regarding the term *rasyā* (palatable): although substances such as jaggery (*guḍa*) possess palatability, they are nonetheless dry; therefore, he says *snigdhā* (unctuous).
Regarding substances such as the froth of milk, although they possess both palatability and unctuousness, they lack stability; therefore, he says *sthirā* (stable).

Regarding substances such as the jackfruit (*panasa*), although they possess palatability, unctuousness, and stability, they are detrimental to the heart and stomach; therefore, he says *hṛdyā hṛd-udara-hitā* (agreeable to the heart and beneficial for the stomach).

Therefore, foods such as those containing cow products, sugar, rice, and wheat should be understood as dear to the *sāttvika* people because they possess the four qualities beginning with deliciousness (*rasyatva*). Furthermore, their *sāttvika* nature is to be understood only when they are indeed beloved by them.
Moreover, since one observes that things may be dear to the *sāttvika* even while possessing these four qualities if they are impure, the qualification "pure" (*pavitra*) must also be added here.
Because of seeing the sight of impure places among those things dear to the tamasic. //8//
Baladeva says: Regarding that, he describes the *sāttvika* food with the words "longevity" (*āyuḥ*) and so forth. Longevity is long life;
*sattva* is steadiness of mind.
Strength is physical capacity;
happiness is satisfaction;
and joy is delight.

The meaning is that rice, wheat, and so forth—which increase these [qualities], possess attributes such as deliciousness, and are accompanied by cow products and sugar—are dear to those of sattva and should be accepted by them.
"Delicious" refers to things like chickpeas which are tasteless;
"unctuous" refers to things like molasses which are dry.

The term "stable" (*sthirā*) excludes unstable things such as the froth of milk and the like; "pleasing to the heart" (*hṛdyā*) excludes unpleasing things such as the jackfruit and the like. Unpleasanthood (*ahṛdyatva*) consists in being harmful to hunger, the stomach, and so forth.
In this context, they should be understood as "purifiers," because even among those things dear to the tamasic, one observes the presence of impure substances. //8//
Bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are dear to those of the passionate nature (rājasa); they bring about pain, grief, and disease. (17.9)
Śrīdhara: Likewise, the word *ati* is connected with all seven [qualities] beginning with *kaṭu*. Therefore, *atikaṭu* refers to the neem tree (*nimbādi*) and similar things.
Excessively sour, excessively salty, and excessively hot are well known.
Excessively pungent refers to black pepper and the like;
excessively dry refers to millet, kodrava, and the like.

Excessively burning foods such as mustard seeds and the like, and excessively pungent foods and so forth, are dear to those of a rajasic nature. Suffering is that which is immediate, such as mental anguish and the like.
Grief (*śoka*) is the mental distress (*daurmanasya*) that occurs subsequently;
illness (*āmaya*) is disease (*roga*). It is so called because it bestows or grants these things. //9//
Madhusūdana:
The word "excessive" (ati) should be applied to all seven [tastes] beginning with pungent (kaṭu).
Pungent is bitter (tikta).
Because the pungent taste (*kaṭu-rasa*) is expressed by the term "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*);
therein, the excessively pungent consists of *nimba* and so forth,
while the excessively sour, salty, and hot are well known.
Excessively sharp [foods] are black pepper and the like;
excessively dry [foods] are devoid of oiliness, such as *kaṅgu* and *kodrava* grains;
and excessively burning [foods] are heat-inducing, such as black mustard seeds and the like.
Suffering (*duḥkha*) is immediate pain;

grief (*śoka*) is the mental distress that occurs subsequently; and disease (*āmaya*) is illness brought about through the imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Foods that provide these are favored by those of a passionate nature (*rājasas*).
By these marks they are to be known as rajasic; the meaning is that they are to be disregarded by those who are sattvic. //9//
Viśvanātha:
The word *ati* is connected with all seven [categories] beginning with *kaṭu*.
*Atikaṭu* refers to the nimba tree and similar substances.
Excessively sour, salty, or hot is well known.
Excessively sharp refers to root-poisons and the like, or black pepper and the like. Excessively dry refers to asafoetida, kodrava grain, and so forth.
"Burning" refers to roasted chickpeas and the like, which cause a burning sensation;
these [foods] bestow suffering and so forth.
In this context, "suffering" is the immediate distress of the tongue, throat, and other parts of the body.
Sorrow (*śoka*) is the dejection that arises subsequently;
affliction (*āmaya*) is disease (*roga*). //9//
Baladeva says: [The text] states that rajasic food is "pungent" (*kaṭu*).
The word *ati-* (excessively) should be applied to all seven [qualities].

Thus, "excessively pungent" refers to bitter substances such as the *nimba* tree and the like, but not to black pepper and the like, because those are designated by the term "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*). It also includes what is excessively sour, excessively salty, and excessively hot.
The well-known *marīci* and similar substances are excessively pungent; *kaṅguka* and similar grains are extremely dry; *rājikā* and similar plants cause excessive burning.
These are favored by those of the *rajas* temperament, but they are to be avoided by those of the *sattva* temperament.
Pain is the immediate suffering born from the parching of the tongue, throat, and so forth;
grief is subsequent mental distress; and disease is the agitation of the blood. (BhG 17.10)
Food that has been kept overnight, its juice gone, putrid, stale, and even that which is leftover or impure—such food is dear to those of a tamasic nature. (10)
Śrīdhara: Likewise, "yāta-yāma" means that of which the *yāma*—the watch or period of three hours—has passed, such as cooked rice and the like;
the meaning is that it has reached a state of coldness.
"Devoid of flavor" means its essence has been squeezed out;
"putrid" means foul-smelling;
"stale" means cooked on another day.
"Ucchiṣṭa" means the remains of what has been eaten by another;
"amedhya" means unfit for consumption, such as *kalañja* and the like.
Food of this nature is dear to the *tāmasa*. //10//

Madhusūdana [explains]: "Yātayāma" means half-cooked, because the term *gatarasa* (devoid of essence) has already been used to denote that which lacks potency; such is the commentary. "Gatarasa" means having reached a state of tastelessness, i.e., dried out.
"Yātayāma" means that which has become cooked and, after being set aside for several hours or more, has reached a state of coldness, such as boiled rice;
others say it refers to milk and the like from which the essence has been extracted, such as churned curds.
"Pūti" means foul-smelling.
"Paryuṣita" refers to that which has been cooked and has remained overnight;
by this, substances such as dhattūra that cause madness when consumed at that time are included.
"Ucchiṣṭa" is that which is well-known as being defiled, namely, what remains after eating.
"Impure" (amedhya) means unfit for sacrifice and unclean, such as meat and the like;
by the word "even" (api ca), that which is declared in the medical treatises to be unwholesome (apathya) is included.
The meaning is that such food—whatever is to be eaten—is dear to one of a tamasic nature and should be utterly shunned by those of a sattvic nature.

It is well known that such food brings about suffering, grief, and disease; therefore, this has not been stated explicitly. Furthermore, in this context, the group beginning with the savory (rasya) is of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), while the group beginning with the pungent (kaṭu) is of the nature of passion (rājasa).
It has been stated that the three groups of food, beginning with *yāta-yāma* (stale), belong to the *tamas* category.
In this regard, one should observe the opposition of the other two groups to the *sattva* group.
For instance, excessive pungency and so forth oppose deliciousness (*rasyatva*), and [excessive] heaviness opposes stability (*sthiratva*).
Excessive heat and so forth are contrary to agreeableness;
the quality of causing disease is contrary to longevity, vitality, strength, and health;
and the quality of causing suffering and grief is contrary to happiness and joy.
Thus, the opposition to the *sāttvika* category within the *rājasa* category is evident.

Likewise, in the *tāmasa* category as well, qualities such as being devoid of flavor (*gata-rasatva*), being stale (*yātayāmatva*), and being kept overnight (*paryuṣitatva*)—as applicable—are opposed to deliciousness (*rasyatva*), unctuousness (*snigdhatva*), and stability (*sthiratva*).
Furthermore, qualities such as being putrid (*pūtitva*), being remnants of a meal (*ucchiṣṭatva*), and being impure (*amedhyatva*) are opposed to being heart-pleasing (*hṛdyatva*).
However, the fact that [these qualities] are contrary to longevity, strength, and so forth, is quite evident.
The distinction is that in the category of the *rājasa* there is only observed contradiction, whereas in the category of the *tāmasa* there is contradiction both observed and unobserved. //10//
Viśvanātha:
"Yāta-yāma" refers to that which has passed its watch or period, such as cooked rice and the like; the meaning is that it has reached a state of coldness.
"Gata-rasa" means that which has lost its natural flavor or whose juice has been squeezed out, such as the skin of a ripe mango or a grape.
*Pūti* means foul-smelling.
*Paryūṣita* means cooked on another day.
*Ucchiṣṭa* means the remains left over after others, such as one's teacher and so forth, have eaten.
"Unclean" refers to things such as *kalañja* that are unfit for consumption.
Therefore, having reflected thus, the sense is that those who desire their own welfare should partake of *sāttvika* food.
However, for Vaiṣṇavas, even that [sāttvika food] must be abandoned if it has not been offered to the Blessed Lord.
It should be understood from the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata that food and other offerings presented to the Blessed One are dear to the world of devotees who are devoid of material qualities. //10//
Baladeva says: He speaks of tamasic food as "yātayāma.
That prepared food, such as cooked grain and the like, for which the *yāma*—the watch or period of three hours—has passed (*yāta*), is *yātayāma*.
It is devoid of flavor and has become insipid.
"Putrid" means foul-smelling;

"stale" means cooked on the previous day; "leftover" means the remains of what has been eaten by others after the teacher has consumed his portion; "impure" means unholy, such as *kalañja* and the like.
Such food is dear to those of a tamasic nature, but it is to be avoided from afar by those of a sattvic nature. //10//

That sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruits, with the mind composed in the thought "sacrifice must indeed be performed," is characterized by goodness (sāttvika). (17.11)
Śrīdhara: Sacrifice (yajña) is also of three kinds.
Among these, he describes the *sāttvika* sacrifice with the words "by those who do not desire fruits.
That sacrifice which is performed—that is, practiced—according to the injunctions prescribed as obligatory by persons free from the desire for fruits, is the *sāttvika* sacrifice.
How is it sacrificed? [The answer is:
"One must simply sacrifice"; the performance of the sacrifice itself is what must be done.
The meaning is that one should fix the mind by concentrating it on the single point [of thought], thinking, "No other fruit is to be accomplished. //11//
Madhusūdana:
Now, with three verses beginning with "aphalākāṅkṣibhiḥ," he describes the threefold sacrifice that has come in its proper sequence.
Sacrifice—consisting of the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, Cāturmāsya, Paśubandha, Jyotiṣṭoma, and so forth—is twofold: optional (kāmya) and obligatory (nitya).

An optional (*kāmya*) rite, impelled by its connection with a specific fruit, must be performed according to the primary method (*mukhya-kalpa*) with the inclusion of all its constituent parts (*sarvāṅga*). A mandatory (*nitya*) rite, however, which is impelled not by a connection with a fruit but by a connection with a cause such as the mere fact of living, may be performed even according to a secondary method (*amukhya-kalpa*) by employing substitutes (*pratinidhi*) and so forth when it is impossible to include all the constituent parts. In that case, even if the inclusion of all parts is impossible, one must certainly perform the sacrifice by employing a substitute, because it is obligatory due to the cause of living and so forth, for the purpose of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*).

Because it is enjoined: having composed the mind and reached a firm decision, those who desire no fruit, seeking the purification of the internal organ (antaḥ-karaṇa) and being averse to rites performed for specific desires, perform—that is, carry out—the sacrifice prescribed by injunction as determined according to the scriptures;
that [sacrifice] is performed according to the scriptures for the sake of purifying the internal organ.
The constant practice being performed in this manner should be known as characterized by sattva. //11//
Viśvanātha:
Now he describes the threefold nature of sacrifice with the words "by those who do not desire fruits.
To the question, "How can there be engagement in sacrifice in the absence of a desire for fruits? he replies: "One must simply sacrifice."
Having composed the mind with the thought, "This must necessarily be performed," because it is prescribed in the scriptures as something to be personally practiced. //11//

Baladeva: Now, with three verses beginning with "aphala," He describes the threefold nature of sacrifice. That sacrifice which is performed—that is, carried out—by those desiring no fruit, meaning those devoid of the desire for results, and which is seen in the injunctions, meaning it arises from the words of the ritual ordinances, is *sāttvika*. [Objection: But how can there be engagement in that without a desire for results? To this He says: "It must simply be sacrificed" (*yaṣṭavyam eva*).

The meaning is: having composed the mind—that is, having made it one-pointed—by resolving that "since this sacrifice has been enjoined by the Veda with respect to me, it must simply be performed, though no fruit is to be attained through it. //11//
But that sacrifice which is performed with a view toward the fruit, and also for the sake of ostentation, O best of the Bharatas— know that sacrifice to be rajasic. 12.
Śrīdhara says: He describes the rajasika sacrifice with the words "abhisandhāya.
That which is performed as a sacrifice—that is, an act of worship—is done with a view toward, or aiming at, a fruit;
and it is for the sake of ostentation and for the purpose of proclaiming one's own greatness.
Know that sacrifice to be of the nature of passion (rājasa). //12//
Madhusūdana:
[One acts] having aimed at or directed toward a desirable fruit such as heaven, but not for the sake of the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*).
The particle *tu* is intended to indicate the distinction from the obligatory (*nitya*) performance.
"Deceit" (*dambha*) in this world means the manifestation of one's own righteousness for that purpose.
Furthermore, the phrase "even so" (*api caiva*) is intended to indicate the threefold nature [of action] through both alternative and cumulative options.

Even though there may be no deceit when one acts with the intention of a transcendent fruit, there are two positions based on the alternative option: that it is indeed for the sake of deceit even when there is no intention for a transcendent fruit.

One position is that [sacrifice] is performed for the sake of both fruits pertaining to the next world and for the sake of worldly hypocrisy; this is the view expressed by the conjunction "also" (*api*).

Thus, know that sacrifice to be *rājasa* which is performed according to the scriptures with an intention toward visible or invisible fruits, without aiming at the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*); O best of the Bharatas, this indicates its unsuitability for the purpose of [liberation]. //12//
Viśvanātha: Nothing. //12//
Baladeva: Know that sacrifice to be rajasic which is performed with a view toward results such as heaven, or out of hypocrisy, or for the purpose of proclaiming one's own greatness. //12//

They declare that sacrifice to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa) which is devoid of scriptural injunctions, where food is not distributed, which lacks mantras, where no priestly fee is given, and which is bereft of faith. 17.13
Śrīdhara says: He describes the *tāmasa* sacrifice with the words "devoid of injunction" (*vidhi-hīnam*).

"Devoid of injunction" means lacking the injunctions prescribed in the scriptures. "Without food distributed" (*asṛṣṭānnam*) means that in which food has not been distributed—that is, not prepared—for the Brahmins and others. It is "devoid of mantras."
The learned declare that a sacrifice which is devoid of the aforementioned sacrificial fees and lacking in faith is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). //13//
Madhusūdana:

The learned describe as *tāmasa* sacrifice that which is contrary to what is taught in the scriptures, devoid of the distribution of food, deficient in its accents and syllables, lacking the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and performed without faith due to hatred toward the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and so forth.

There are six types [of tamasic sacrifice]: fivefold, characterized by each individual attribute such as deficiency in ritual procedure (*vidhi-hīnatva*) and so forth, and one type characterized by the combination of all attributes.
Furthermore, many other varieties of tamasic sacrifice are to be understood through the combination of two, three, or four attributes.

In the rajasic sacrifice, although there is no purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*), there exists a *apūrva* (unseen potency) that produces results due to performance according to the scriptures.
In the case of the *tāmasa* [action], however, because it is performed contrary to the scriptures, there is no extraordinary result (*apūrva*); this is the distinction. //13//
Viśvanātha:
"Asṛṣṭānna" means devoid of the gift of food. //13//

Baladeva: "Vidhi" means that which is without prepared food—that is, devoid of the gift of food—and accompanied by a mantra that is deficient in accent and phoneme, and is further lacking in faith due to hatred toward the officiating priests. //13//
Worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, straightforwardness, celibacy, and non-violence—this is called bodily austerity. //14//

Śrīdhara: In order to demonstrate the divisions of austerity (tapas) into sāttvika and so forth, he first states its threefold nature according to the distinctions of bodily and other types in the three verses beginning with "deva...".
Among these, he describes the bodily [tapaḥ] with the words "deva...";
here, "prājñāḥ" refers to others who know the truth, excluding the Guru and the Vyakti.
The worship of gods, Brahmins, and others, as well as physical purification and so forth, which are performed by means of the body, is called bodily austerity (śārīra-tapas). //14//
Madhusūdana:

In order to explain the divisions of austerity (tapas) according to the qualities of sattva and so forth as they occur in sequence, he describes its threefold nature—distinguished by body, speech, and mind—in three verses beginning with "devair" (by the gods).
The gods (devāḥ) are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, Agni, Durgā, and others.
The twice-born (dvija) are the best of the twice-born, the Brahmins;
the gurus are fathers, mothers, teachers, and so forth;
the wise (prājña) are the learned (paṇḍita), those who have understood the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Their worship consists of prostration, service, and so forth, according to the scriptures.
Purity is the cleansing of the body with earth and water.
Straightforwardness is the absence of crookedness; this will be described under mental austerity by the term "purity of disposition."

Physical integrity (*ārjava*) consists in acting and refraining in a uniform manner regarding what is prescribed and what is prohibited. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the abstention from forbidden sexual intercourse.
Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the absence of harming living beings as enjoined by the scriptures.
By the inclusion of the word "and" (ca), non-stealing and non-possessiveness are also included.
Physical action is that which is accomplished by means of the body as the primary instrument, along with the agent and other factors, but not by the body alone;
for he will state later: "These five are its causes."
Thus is austerity of the body described. //14//
Viśvanātha:
While describing the threefold nature of austerity (*tapas*), he first states the threefold nature of *sāttvika* austerity with the three verses beginning with "The Lord" (*deva*). //14//

Baladeva: In order to explain the divisions of austerity (*tapas*)—such as the *sāttvika* and others—which follows in sequence, [the Lord] first states its threefold nature according to the bodily and other modes by means of three verses beginning with "devā. Here, "devas" refers to the Vasus, Rudras, and so forth; "dvijas" refers to the best of Brahmins; "gurus" refers to mothers, fathers, and teachers; and "prājñas" refers to those who have mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas. "Others" refers to their worship. Purity (*śauca*) has been described as being of two kinds.

Straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is the state of engaging in prescribed actions and desisting from prohibited ones with a single-minded consistency. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the practice of sexual restraint as prescribed.
This is bodily austerity (*śārīra-tapas*), which is accomplished by means of the body. (14)
Speech that causes no agitation, which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, as well as the practice of reciting one's own sacred texts— this is called austerity of speech (vāṅ-maya tapas). 17.15
Śrīdhara says: He describes verbal austerity with the words "not causing agitation.
A statement that does not produce agitation—that is, fear—is "not causing agitation" (anudvegakara). It is truthful and pleasing to the listener.
The practice of recitation and the study of the Vedas—which are beneficial and result in happiness—are the austerity consisting of speech, which is accomplished by means of speech. //15//
Madhusūdana:
[That which is] not causing agitation is that which causes no suffering to anyone;
it is truth, rooted in valid means of knowledge, and its meaning is uncontradicted.
It is pleasant to hear, providing immediate auditory pleasure, beneficial, and bringing happiness in its ultimate result.
The particle *ca* serves to aggregate these qualifiers;
it is distinguished by this fourfold set of attributes—beginning with "not causing distress"—and is not deficient even by a single qualifier.
Any speech such as, "Be peaceful, my child; practice sacred study and yoga, and thus it will be for your welfare," and so forth—that is vocal austerity (*vāṅ-maya tapas*), like bodily austerity.
Furthermore, the practice of sacred study and the study of the Vedas according to the rules are called vocal austerity.
The particle *eva* is to be explained here as serving to restrict the conjunction of the preceding qualifiers. //15//
Viśvanātha:
[It is] not causing agitation; it does not cause agitation even for those who are different from the intended audience. //15//
Baladeva: [Speech that is] not causing agitation—that which produces no fear or distress in anyone;
truthful—consistent with valid means of knowledge;
and pleasing to the listener.
And beneficial in its ultimate transformation.

A sentence possessing these four qualifications, as well as the study of one's own Veda—the practice of the Vedas—is austerity consisting of speech (*vāṅ-maya*), which is accomplished by means of speech. //15//
Tranquility of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, and purity of being— this is called mental austerity (mānasa-tapas). 16.
Śrīdhara says that he describes mental austerity as "serenity of mind" (*manaḥ-prasāda*). Serenity of mind is clarity;
it is gentleness and the absence of cruelty.
Mauna is the state of a sage; its meaning is "reflection. It is the restraint of the self and the mind, the withdrawal [of them] from sense objects.
Purity of disposition is the absence of deceit in one's conduct;
this is mental austerity. //16//
Madhusūdana:
Serenity of mind is clarity and transparency, being free from agitation caused by thoughts of sense objects;
gentleness is mildness, the desire for the welfare of all the world, and the absence of thinking about what is prohibited.

Mauna is the state of a sage (muni-bhāva), which consists of self-contemplation through one-pointedness known as *nididhyāsana*. According to the Bhāṣya, mauna is the restraint of the mind that serves as the cause for the restraint of speech. Self-restraint (*ātma-vinigraha*) is the specific restraint or cessation of all modifications of the mind—that is, the *asamprajñāta* samādhi.
The purification of the heart (*bhāva-śuddhi*) is the removal of impurities such as desire, anger, and greed.
Furthermore, that purity of being (bhāva-śuddhi) is distinguished by its correctness, which consists in being free from the arising of impurity;
the commentary states that this is the absence of deceit (māyā) during the time of social interaction with others.
This kind of austerity is called mental (mānasa). //16//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: Serenity of mind, purity, freedom from distraction regarding the recollection of sense objects, gentleness, lack of cruelty, and the desire for the happiness of all.
Silence is reflection upon the Self;
restraint of the mind is the withdrawal of the self from sense objects;
purity of being is sincerity in one's conduct.
Thus, this austerity is to be accomplished by means of the mind. //16//
That threefold austerity (tapas) performed by men with supreme faith, by those who are disciplined and free from desire for rewards, is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). 17.17.
Śrīdhara: Thus, the threefold austerity (tapas) to be accomplished by means of body, speech, and mind has been shown.
He now describes the threefold nature of each of these three types of austerity according to the divisions of *sāttvika* and so forth, beginning with the verse starting "with faith" (*śraddhayā*).

They declare that even this threefold austerity is *sāttvika* when it is performed by men who possess supreme—that is, excellent—faith, who are free from desire for results, and whose minds are disciplined and one-pointed. (17)
Madhusūdana:

Now, with the three verses beginning with "śraddhayā," He demonstrates the threefold division—sāttvika and so forth—of the aforementioned austerity (tapas), which is said to be of three kinds according to its distinctions as bodily, vocal, and mental.
That previously mentioned threefold austerity—bodily, vocal, and mental—is [performed] with faith, that is, with a conviction in the existence of the unseen.

The learned declare that action performed by qualified persons who are endowed with supreme excellence, free from the stain of doubt regarding its validity, devoid of desire for rewards, disciplined, composed, and remaining unchanged in success or failure, is *sāttvika*. //17//
Viśvanātha:
[The threefold] is that which has been described by the aforementioned definition, consisting of the physical, vocal, and mental. //17//
Baladeva: He describes the threefold nature of the aforementioned austerity according to its *sāttvika* and other qualities with these three verses.

It has been said: that threefold austerity which is performed and practiced with supreme faith by men who are free from desire for fruits, who are disciplined, and whose minds are one-pointed, is *sāttvika*. (17)
That austerity which is performed here with hypocrisy for the sake of honor, respect, and worship, is declared to be rajasic; it is unstable and impermanent. (17.18)
Śrīdhara says that [the verse] describes the *rājasa* [type]:
"Satkāra" is verbal worship, such as saying "this person is virtuous" or "this is an ascetic," and so forth; "māna" is physical worship, such as rising to greet or saluting.
It is for the sake of honor, gain, and so forth;
it is the austerity performed for such purposes and with hypocrisy.
For this very reason, it is unstable and uncertain.
And that austerity which is unstable and momentary—such as this is declared here to be rajasic. //18//
Madhusūdana:
"Honor" refers to praise such as "this ascetic is a virtuous Brahmin," performed by those lacking discrimination;
"respect" refers to rising to meet him, saluting him, and so forth.
Pūjā consists of washing the feet, worship, giving wealth, and so forth.

That austerity which is performed for the sake of such [pūjā] solely out of hypocrisy and merely by bearing the banner of dharma (*dharma-dhvajitva*), and not with a sense of faith (*āstikya-buddhi*), is declared by the learned to be *rājasa*.
It yields fruit only in this very world and not in the next; it is unstable, its fruit lasting for only a very short time.
Non-firm means being devoid of the necessity of producing a result. //18//
Viśvanātha:
"This person is virtuous"—thus another should perform verbal worship (*vāk-pūjā*).
"He is worthy of honor"—through rising to meet him, saluting him, and other such acts, another should perform physical worship (*daihikī pūjā*).
Worship is that which is performed with wealth and other offerings given by others, or it is mental worship for that purpose;
and that austerity which is performed out of hypocrisy is rajasic.
It is fickle, lasting only for a short time.
It is unstable, having as its fruit rewards such as honor and so forth that are not certain. //18//
Baladeva: "Satkāra" is praise such as "this ascetic is virtuous.
"Māna" is respect, such as rising to greet him and so forth.

"Pūjā" is the washing of his feet, the giving of wealth, and the like. That austerity which is performed for the sake of these [praises, respect, and worship] and with hypocrisy is declared to be *rājasa*.
Fickle means temporary;
unstable means having uncertain results such as honor and the like. //18//
That austerity which is performed with a deluded grasp, causing pain to oneself or for the purpose of destroying another, is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). //19//
Śrīdhara says: He describes tamasic austerity with the words "by foolish persistence" (mūḍha).

That austerity which is performed by means of self-inflicted pain through a foolish obsession—that is, a dogmatic insistence born of non-discrimination—or for the purpose of destroying another, that is, for the sake of the ruin of someone else in the form of malevolent magic (abhicāra), is declared, or spoken of, as tamasic. //19//

Madhusūdana: That austerity which is performed with a stubborn insistence born of extreme lack of discrimination— that is, through the affliction of one's own aggregate of body and senses— either for the purpose of destroying another, for the purpose of annihilating someone else, or in the form of malevolent magic (abhicāra), that is tāmasa.
This has been declared by the learned. //19//
Viśvanātha:
By "grasping with delusion" (mūḍha-grāheṇa), he means by the seizing upon ignorance;
for the sake of the destruction—that is, the ruin—of another. //19//

Baladeva: That austerity which is performed with a foolish grasp—that is, with a lack of discrimination born of stubbornness—and which causes pain to oneself, the body, and the senses, for the sake of destroying or ruining another, is *tāmasa* (BG 17.20).
As for the gift which is given with the thought "it ought to be given" to one who does not return the favor;
That gift given at the right place, at the right time, and to a worthy recipient is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). //20//
Śrīdhara: He states the threefold nature of giving, which was previously promised, with the words "it must be given" (*dātavyam*).

That gift which is given with the firm resolve that "it simply must be given" to one who does not provide assistance, yet is capable of returning it, at a proper place such as Kurukṣetra and so forth, and at a proper time such as during an eclipse and so forth.

The locative case is employed here due to the association with place and time; "in a worthy recipient" (pātre) means to a Brāhmaṇa who has become a worthy recipient, being endowed with austerity, sacred learning, and so forth. Alternatively, "pātre" is a form ending in the suffix -tṛc (meaning "one who is").
The meaning is "to the protector.
This is indeed the dative case;
for he protects (pāti) the giver from every multitude of calamities, and thus he is a protector (pātā).
That gift which is of such a nature for him is sattvic. //20//
Madhusūdana:
Now, with three verses beginning with "dātavyam," he shows the threefold nature of giving (*dāna*) as it follows in sequence.

Giving is that which is bestowed upon one who does not return the favor—that is, one who produces no reciprocal benefit—out of a firm resolve that "it must simply be given" by virtue of the injunctions of the scriptures, and not out of a desire for a fruit (*phala*), such as the *tulā-puruṣa* sacrifice and others.
In a sacred place such as Kurukṣetra and so forth, at a sacred time such as a solar eclipse and so forth, and to a worthy recipient—
here the locative case is used in the sense of the dative—
to what kind of recipient? To one who does not seek personal gain and who is endowed with learning and austerity.
Or [one may give] "to the protector of the vessel.
According to the scripture, one should accept only that which is capable of protecting both oneself and the donor through knowledge and austerity;
such a gift is declared to be *sāttvika*. (20)
Viśvanātha:
That gift which is given with the firm resolve that "it must be given," and not with a view toward the fruit [of the action]. //20//
Baladeva: Now he describes the threefold nature of giving with the words "it should be given.

That gift which is given with a firm resolve to a worthy recipient (*pātra*) who does not return the favor—a Brāhmaṇa who protects the giver through his learning and austerity—that gift is *sāttvika*.
"To one who does not return the favor" means without aiming for a reciprocal benefit.
In a sacred place, at a holy site, at the proper time, and on occasions such as the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), etc. //20//
But that gift which is given for the sake of a return favor, or with a specific fruit in view, and which is given with a sense of distress— that gift is declared to be rajasic. 17.21
Śrīdhara says: He describes the *rājasa* gift with the word "that which.

That gift which is given again—either for the purpose that "this person will benefit me at a later time," or aiming for a fruit such as heaven—and which is "distressed," meaning it is accompanied by mental affliction (*citta-kleśa*), is of such a nature.
Such a gift is declared to be "king-like" (rājasa). //21//
Madhusūdana:

That gift which is given for the sake of a return favor—thinking, "He will assist me at a later time"—or with a view toward a visible result such as heaven and the like, is distinct from the *sāttvika* type; it is given with distress, thinking, "How much has been spent!"
Thus, that gift which is given in such a way as to be accompanied by subsequent regret is declared to be of the nature of passion (rājasa). //21//
Viśvanātha:
"Extremely distressed" means being filled with remorse, thinking, "How is it that so much has been spent?
Alternatively, it means that even in the absence of a desire to give, [the gift] was given solely due to the constraint of the command of elders and others.
It is afflicted and characterized by unwholesome substances and actions. //21//

Baladeva: That gift which is given for the sake of a return favor, for the sake of a visible result, or aiming at and intending an invisible result such as heaven and so forth, is *rājasa*. That which is given with distress—meaning accompanied by regret, thinking "How much must be spent!"—or out of compliance with the words of a superior, is *rājasa*. //21//
That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients, without respect and with contempt— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). 17.22.
Śrīdhara says: He describes the *tāmasa* gift with the words "adeśe" and so forth. "Adeśe" means in an impure place;
"akāle" means at a time of impurity and the like.

That gift which is given to unworthy recipients—such as libertines, actors, dancers, and the like—even when there is excellence of place, time, and recipient; which is offered without respect, devoid of honors such as washing the feet and so forth;
and which is treated with contempt, involving a disregard for the recipient.
Giving performed in such a manner is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). //22//
Madhusūdana:
In an improper place—either by its own nature, through association with wicked people, or because it is a cause of sin, such as an impure location;
or at an improper time—anything whatsoever that is not recognized as being a cause of merit.
Or [that which is given] during a period of impurity;

or that gift which is given to unworthy recipients—such as actors, lechers, and the like—who are devoid of learning and austerity; or even when there is excellence of place, time, and recipient, it is given without respect, lacking honor such as pleasant speech, washing of the feet, and worship, being instead accompanied by contempt and disregard for the recipient.
And that gift is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). //22//
Viśvanātha:
Insult is the fruit of contempt. //22//
Baladeva says: that which is given to unworthy recipients, such as actors and the like, at an improper place— that is, an impure location— and at an improper time— that is, an impure occasion.

Even when there is excellence of place and other factors, that gift which is offered without respect—devoid of honors such as washing the feet, treated with contempt, and accompanied by disrespectful speech such as "tūṅkāra"—is tāmasa. //22//
"Oṃ Tat Sat"—this is remembered as the threefold designation of Brahman.
By means of this, the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices were ordained in ancient times. (17.23)
Therefore, having uttered "Om," the acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity, as prescribed by the rules, are constantly performed by those who discourse on Brahman. (24)

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object that if this were the case, then all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and so forth would consist primarily of the qualities of passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas), and thus the exertion involved in sacrifices and the like would be futile.
Anticipating this objection, the Lord says "Om" in order to demonstrate the manner in which even such acts can be established as being characterized by goodness (sattva).
"Oṃ tat sat"—this threefold designation, this naming and description of Brahman, the Supreme Self, is recorded by the learned.
Among these, "Oṃ" is the name of Brahman because of its well-known status in such Vedic texts as "Oṃ is Brahman.
Furthermore, the word "tat" (That) is also a name for Brahman, because it is universally renowned as the cause of the universe and is beyond the perception of the ignorant.

The word *sat* (Being) is also a name for Brahman, because of its qualities such as ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sattva*), goodness (*sādhutva*), and excellence (*praśastatva*), according to such Vedic scriptures as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sad eva somyedam agra āsīt*). These three types [of names] were designated by the Creator at the beginning of the creation; thus, the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices were ordained and fashioned by the Ordainer.
Or, it may mean "endowed with qualities.
For example, by that Supreme Self who possesses this threefold designation, the Brāhmaṇas and others were created as the most pure.
Therefore, this threefold exposition of it is highly commendable; such is the meaning. //23//
Now, intending to demonstrate the excellence of each [syllable] beginning with *oṃ*, he speaks of that very thing regarding *oṃ* with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since the designation of Brahman as such is thus praised, therefore, having uttered— that is, pronounced— "oṃ," the ritual acts of those who recite the Vedas, such as sacrifices and the like, which are prescribed by the scriptures, always— that is, at all times— even when there is a deficiency in the constituent parts (*aṅga*), proceed with excellence.
The meaning is that they become possessed of qualities. //24//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, by describing the threefold nature of food, sacrifice, austerity, and charity, it has been stated that those which are *sāttvika* should be accepted, while those which are *rājasa* and *tāmasa* should be avoided.
In that regard, since food serves a visible purpose, there is no apprehension of a failure of results due to defects in its constituent parts.

However, in the case of sacrifices, austerities, and gifts whose purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there would be an absence of fruit due to the non-arising of the *apūrva* when there is a deficiency in their constituent parts. Thus, even for those actions performed with a predominance of *sattva*, futility would result because performers are prone to many errors.
Therefore, to avoid such deficiencies, there is a general expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of the utterance of the Lord’s name: "Oṃ Tat Sat."
Out of supreme compassion, the Blessed One teaches: "Oṃ.

That which is of the form "Oṃ tat sat" is the designation (*nirdeśa*) of Brahman, the Supreme Self; it is called a "designation" because by means of this [syllable] there is a pointing out—that is to say, it is the expressive word or name. It is known as "threefold" (*trividha*) by those learned in the Vedānta, meaning that which possesses three modes or constituent parts.
Because it is stated in the singular, a single name consists of three parts,
like the *praṇava*.
Since this was recorded by the great seers of old as an instruction regarding Brahman, the injunction is here inferred that it must likewise be remembered by those of the present day.
This is because of the principle that "declarations such as 'the first portion belongs to the one who utters *vaṣaṭ*'" apply only when there is no prior rule (*apūrvatvāt*).

Furthermore, because of its connection with the acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity, its fruit is precisely the non-deficiency (*avaiguṇya*) of those acts; this is inferred through mutual requirement (*parasparākāṅkṣayā*), like the case of a horse and a chariot that have been burnt together. [As stated:
"Whatever part of the ritual act performed during sacrifices may fall away due to negligence..."
"By the mere remembrance of that Viṣṇu, [the sacrifice] becomes complete"—so says the Śruti.
Thus, according to this Smṛti and likewise from the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*),
the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is praised for the purpose of stating their capacity to prevent defects in ritual action (*karma-vaiguṇya*).
The term "Brāhmaṇas" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for members of all three twice-born classes (*traivarṇika*).

The Brahmins and others are the agents, the Vedas are the instruments, and the sacrifices are the actions; these were ordained in the past by Prajāpati through that instruction of Brahman which served as the instrument.
Therefore, the meaning is that this instruction possesses great power, being capable of remedying any deficiency because it is the cause of the creation of sacrifices and other rites. //23//

Now, just as the syllable *oṃ* is explained by means of an explanation of its constituent parts— the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*— he begins to explain with four verses the designation of Brahman as the composite form of those [letters] through an explanation of the words *oṃ*, *tat*, and *sat*, in order to heighten the praise. Among these, he first explains the word *oṃ* with the verse beginning "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Since the name "Om" is well-known as that of Brahman in such scriptural passages as "Om is Brahman," therefore, having uttered "Om"— that is,

immediately after the pronunciation of the syllable Om— the sacrificial, charitable, and ascetic acts prescribed by the injunctions taught in the ritual scriptures proceed constantly and preeminently, free from deficiency, for those who speak of Brahman and those who speak of the Vedas.
Since there is no deficiency even from the utterance of a single constituent part, how much less so from the utterance of it in its entirety; such is the excellence of the praise. //24//
Viśvanātha:
Thus, the threefold nature of austerity, sacrifice, and so forth has been described in general with respect to all human beings.

Among those who follow the path of goodness (sāttvika), however, for those who are seekers of Brahman (brahmavādins), sacrifices and other rites must be preceded by the designation of Brahman; thus he says: "Oṃ Tat Sat"—such is the designation of Brahman.
Designation by name is traditionally recorded as that which has been taught by the learned.
In this regard, "Om" is indeed well-known in all the Vedas as the name of Brahman.
It is called *tat* because it is well-known as the cause of the universe, and because it is established by the refutation of what is not that;
and it is called *sat* because of the Vedic scripture: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sad eva somyedam agra āsīt*).
For it is by Brahman alone—denoted by the words *oṃ*, *tat*, and *sat*—that the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices were ordained and brought into being.
Therefore, having uttered and pronounced "Om," which is the name of Brahman, the sacrifices and other rites of those who profess Brahman proceed. //23-24//

Baladeva: Thus, by explaining the threefold nature of austerity, sacrifice, and charity, it has been shown that those which are characterized by *sattva* are to be adopted, while those characterized by *rajas* and *tamas* are to be abandoned.
Now, it is stated—indeed—that for those qualified by *sattva*, sacrifices and other rites must be preceded by the name of Viṣṇu. Om.
The threefold designation of Brahmā-Viṣṇu beginning with "Om" is recorded by the learned as his name;
for the Śruti states, "Om—this is the name of Brahmā that is nearest. Thus, "Om" is the single name.
"Thou art That," according to this Vedic scripture, "That" (tat) is the second name; "Being alone, my dear," according to this Vedic scripture, "Being" (sat) is the third name.
This is intended as an illustration.

By that threefold designation of the names Viṣṇu and others, the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices were ordained and revealed in the past by the Four-faced One (Brahmā); therefore, this designation possesses great power, and there is no deficiency in the constituent parts of the sacrifices and other rites preceded by it, nor is there any deficiency in their results. //23//

Since this is so, therefore, having uttered and pronounced the instruction "Om," the ritual acts such as sacrifices performed by the three classes of Brahminical speakers—who are characterized by sattva—proceed;
even when there is a deficiency in their constituent parts, they attain completeness. //24//
BG 17.25: Actions of sacrifice, austerity, and various acts of charity are performed by those desiring liberation, without aiming for their fruits, [thinking] "This is [the right thing to do]."
Śrīdhara: He introduces the second name; "that" (tat) means "having uttered 'that'. This is to be construed with the preceding [verse].
Having uttered—that is, having pronounced—"that," actions such as sacrifice are performed by persons of pure mind who desire liberation, without forming an attachment to results.

Therefore, because it brings about the state of one desiring liberation by means of purifying the mind through the abandonment of the intention for fruits, the designation by the word "that" is praiseworthy; this is the meaning. //25//
Madhusūdana explains the second occurrence of the word "tat" as follows:

having cited "tat" as a name of Brahman, well-known from such scriptural passages as "That thou art" (tattvam asi), [one should practice] without aiming for any fruit, for the sake of purifying the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
Sacrificial rites, austerities, and various acts of charity are performed by those desiring liberation; therefore, this [knowledge] is most highly praised. //25//
Viśvanātha: The word "tat" (that) is to be connected with the preceding phrase "having uttered. "Without intending the fruit" means without forming an intention for a result. //25//
Baladeva: Citing that designation, [it is said that] rites such as sacrifice are performed and practiced by those desiring liberation without aiming for rewards.
Because it accomplishes the desire for liberation through freedom from desire, that word [the word "That"] possesses great power. //26//
The word *sat* is used in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness; likewise, O Pārtha, the word *sat* is applied to a praiseworthy action. (17.26)
Abiding in sacrifice, austerity, and charity is called "Good" (sat); and action performed for that purpose is likewise designated as "Good. (27)
Śrīdhara: With the two verses beginning with "sad-bhāve," he explains the excellence of the word *sat*.
"In the sense of *sad-bhāve*" means in the sense of existence;
that is, in the sense that Devadatta has a son and so forth.
The word *sat* is employed in the sense of goodness (*sādhu-bhāva*) and excellence (*sādhutva*), that is,
in the meaning "I am the foremost among the sons and so forth of Devadatta."

In praiseworthy and auspicious rites such as marriage and the like, the word *sat* is employed in the sense that "this action is good" (*sat-karma*), or it is used because it "accords with reality" (*saṅgacchate*). //26//
Furthermore, regarding the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*):
that state of being established with single-minded devotion in sacrifices and other such acts is also called "Being" (*sat*).

Whatever action—such as worship, offerings, sweeping and smearing the courtyard of the house, or preparing the arena for auspicious rites—is performed for the sake of that which possesses these three names, its true object and fruit is that very Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thus, that action is "for the sake of That" (*tadartha*).
Whatever other action is performed for the sake of accomplishing that [primary goal]— such as actions concerning gardens, rice fields, or the acquisition of wealth—
that action is "for the sake of that" (tad-arthīya).
And even though it is extremely remote, it is designated simply as "existent."

Since these three names are thus exceedingly praiseworthy, the intended meaning is that one should recite them for the sake of the successful completion of all ritual actions (*sarva-karma-sādguṇya*). In this context, an injunction (*vidhi*) is inferred because the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) would otherwise be illogical; according to the maxim, "the object to be enjoined is praised."

Others, however, say that passages such as "others proceed" or "are performed by those desiring liberation," which employ the present tense, must be transformed into injunctions—just like "he sacrifices with fuel"—but this is not tenable because [the meaning] is already established in cases such as "in the state of being good" (*sad-bhāve*) or "in the state of being virtuous" (*sādhu-bhāve*);
therefore, the assumption of an injunction according to the previously stated method is superior. //27//
Madhusūdana explains the third word, *sat*, with two verses: "In the sense of 'existence' (*sad-bhāva*).
This term *sat*—well-known from such Vedic passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sad eva somyedam agra āsīt*)—is a name of Brahman in the sense of existence.

When there is a doubt as to existence regarding that which exists, and a doubt as to correctness regarding that which is correct, this [word] is employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) to establish its correctness and the existence of its result by removing defects. Therefore, the meaning is that this [word] is capable of ensuring the correctness of sacrifices and the like, as well as the existence of their fruit.

Likewise, O Pārtha, the word *sat* is appropriately used—just as in the cases of existence and correctness—in reference to an auspicious rite such as a marriage, which is praiseworthy and productive of immediate happiness without obstruction.

Therefore, the meaning is that this name is more praiseworthy because it is capable of producing swift results through the removal of defects by means of sacrifice and other such acts, without any obstruction. //26//
That steadfastness— remaining intent upon sacrifice, austerity, and charity— is also called "good" by the wise.
And action for their sake— that is, action pertaining to those objects consisting of sacrifice, charity, and austerity,
or action performed with the intention of offering them to the Blessed One— is likewise "for their sake."
It is indeed designated as "Sat" (Being).
Therefore, the name "Sat" is most excellent, for it is capable of dispelling defects in ritual action.
If even each single part of this [mantra] is such, what need is there to speak of the majesty of its totality—the designation "Oṃ Tat Sat"? This is the summarized meaning. //27//
Viśvanātha:
The word *sat*, which denotes Brahman, is also used in the sense of "praiseworthy.

Therefore, with the intention that the word *sat* should be employed for any praiseworthy action, whether material (*prākṛta*) or non-material (*aprākṛta*), he says "the state of being existent" (*sad-bhāva*) in two verses.

The meaning is that it is applied in the sense of being in a state of goodness, in the state of Brahman, in the state of being virtuous, and in the state of being a speaker of Brahman; that is to say, it is consistent with these. "Abiding in sacrifice and so forth" means remaining intent upon sacrifice and the like.
"Action for that purpose" refers even to those actions conducive to the practice of *brahmacarya*, such as the cleaning of the Lord’s temple and so on. (26–27)

Baladeva: The term "sat" (existent) is employed in reference to various praiseworthy objects; therefore, with the intention that it should be applied to every praiseworthy action, he says, by means of two verses, "the state of being existent" (*sad-bhāva*).

The word "sat" is used as a designator for the state of being existent (*sad-bhāva*), the state of being Brahman (*brahma-bhāva*), and the state of being virtuous (*sādhu-bhāva*), which is to say, the state of knowing Brahman—as in passages such as "That which is existent, my dear... (*sad eva saumya...*) and "From association with the virtuous" (*satāṃ prasaṅgāt...*).
Likewise, the word *sat* is appropriately applied and consistent with auspicious rites such as the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*) and marriage.
Furthermore, their state during sacrifices and other rituals—their focused persistence therein—is also called *sat*.
Any action pertaining to that [Brahman] whose three names are these—such as the construction of its temple or its cleansing—is designated as *sat*.
In this context, the injunction "this threefold instruction is to be remembered" is to be inferred;

for, according to the principle that "statements [concerning] the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer [are primary] because they are unprecedented (*apūrva*)," and because of its connection with sacrifice, giving, and so forth, the result of this [omission] is indeed a deficiency in those acts.
"Whatever part of the ritual in the sacrifices might fall away from those performing it through negligence..."
"By the mere remembrance of that Viṣṇu, it becomes complete"—thus says the Śruti.
And because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa). //26–27//
Whatever is offered, given, or performed as austerity without faith, O Pārtha, is called "unreal" (asat); it yields no fruit either after death or in this world. (17.28)

Śrīdhara: Now, in order to show that one should engage in all actions with faith alone, he censures everything performed without faith, beginning with the words "aśraddhayā" (without faith). "Hutam" refers to an oblation;
"dattam" refers to a gift.
The austerity performed has ceased,
as have whatever other actions were done;
all that is said to be non-existent because, due to its deficiency, it does not bear fruit after death in another world.
It does not bear fruit here, nor in this world, because it results in infamy.

Having abandoned faith consisting of passion and ignorance, and having resorted to faith consisting of goodness, one becomes qualified for the knowledge of reality; thus it is established in the seventeenth chapter.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Division of the Three Kinds of Faith," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Madhusūdana:

If, due to laziness or other such causes, one sets aside the scriptural injunction and performs sacrifice, austerity, charity, and so forth merely out of faith by following the practice of the elders, and if a deficiency occurs through negligence, [it is remedied] by the designation of Brahman as "Oṃ Tat Sat."

[Objection: In that case, even for the Asuras—who, out of lack of faith, abandon the scriptural injunction and perform some sacrifice or other according to their own whims—there would be a removal of defects by that very same [performance]; thus, what is the use of faith, which is the cause of being characterized by *sattva*? To this, he says: "By lack of faith... (aśraddhayā).

Whatever oblation has been offered into the fire, whatever has been given to Brāhmaṇas, whatever austerity has been practiced, and whatever other action has been performed— such as praise, prostration, and so forth— if done without faith,
all that is said to be "unreal" (asat) and "not good" (asādhu).
For this very reason, its goodness cannot be produced by the designation "Oṃ Tat Sat," because it is in every way unfit for such a state, just as a sprout cannot grow from a stone.
Why is that said to be "non-existent"? Listen, O Pārtha!
The word *ca* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Because that which is performed without faith does not bear fruit after death in the next world, since, being deficient in quality, it does not produce the unseen merit (*apūrva*).

Neither here nor in this world is there glory for one who acts out of lack of faith, because such a person is censured by the virtuous. Therefore, since it is devoid of both worldly and otherworldly fruits, one should perform sacrifices and other rites with *sāttvika* faith alone for the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The ultimate point is that when there is apprehension of deficiency due to fate regarding such *sāttvika* sacrifices and other acts performed with faith, their perfection should be secured by invoking the name of Brahman.

The Commentary states that even sacrifices and other rites performed without *sattva*, though deficient due to a lack of faith, become endowed with *sattva* and possessed of merit through the invocation of the name of Brahman.

Thus, in this chapter, it is shown that those who disregard the scriptures out of laziness and the like, yet proceed with acts based merely on the traditional practice of elders and motivated by faith, exhibit the nature of *asuras* due to their disregard for scripture, while simultaneously exhibiting the nature of *devas* through their performance of acts preceded by faith.

Are these beings Asuras or Devas? For those whose objects of doubt concern Arjuna, it is shown—by means of demonstrating the threefold nature of faith and the threefold nature of food and so forth—that those who perform sacrifices and other rites with rājasa and tāmasa faith are Asuras, being ineligible for the means of scriptural knowledge; whereas those who perform sacrifices and other rites with sāttvika faith are Devas, being eligible for the means of scriptural knowledge.
It is established that the Blessed One has made a definitive determination. //28//

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Division of the Threefold Faith," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā), composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Viśveśvara Sarasvatī.
Viśvanātha:
"Good action" refers to that which is prescribed by the scriptures.
In response to the inquiry as to what "bad action" is, he says: "by lack of faith."
The oblation has been offered;
the gift has been given;
the austerity has been practiced.

Whatever other action has been performed, all that is non-existent; even what is offered is as if unoffered, even what is given is as if ungiven, even austerity is as if unpracticed, and even what is done is as if undone.
Because that [action] bears fruit neither after death in the next world, nor does it bear fruit in this world. //28//
Among the various types of actions mentioned, that which is performed with faith and characterized by sattva alone is fit for liberation; this is the meaning declared in this chapter.
Thus, in this *Harṣiṇī* commentary that showers the essence of meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, this seventeenth chapter has been properly concluded for the virtuous. 17.
Baladeva: Now, one should engage in all actions with faith characterized by goodness (*sāttvikī śraddhā*).
He censures the absence of such faith with the words "without faith" (*aśraddhayā*), stating that everything [done] without it is futile;
*hutam* refers to the oblation.
The gift that was given,
the austerity that was practiced, and whatever other action such as praise or prostration was performed— all that is said to be non-existent and censurable.
To the question "Why?", he says: "And not...

The word "and" (*ca*) is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*), because that which is performed without faith does not bear fruit after death in the next world due to its deficiency; nor does it bring fame in this world because it is censured by the virtuous. //28//
Having abandoned faith born of one's own nature and having relied upon that which is born of scripture, one becomes entitled to the supreme good; such is the seventeenth position.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad.
